name: Modern Pop
blurb: From Mariah to Olivia: the hit makers and happy accidents of modern pop.

stories.title: The Swedish Hit Factory
stories.dek: How a Stockholm studio taught radio how to build a pop song
stories.body:
In the early 1990s a small Stockholm studio called Cheiron became the quiet engine room of world pop. Its founder, a DJ turned producer who called himself Denniz PoP, had a feel for hooks that were bright, simple and impossible to forget. Working with him was a young musician named Karl Martin Sandberg, who had sung in a Swedish hard-rock band called It's Alive. He took the name Max Martin, and he and PoP began writing songs together.

The sound they built was careful and cold-eyed. Martin has described writing melodies first and fitting words to them afterward, sometimes picking syllables for how they felt in the mouth rather than for meaning. That habit helps explain why lines from their songs stick even when the words are odd. Their studio also worked quickly, turning out demos that singers could learn in an afternoon.

Cheiron's early hits came from acts such as Ace of Base, and then the Backstreet Boys, whose early singles were recorded in Stockholm. Then, in 1997, Martin and his colleague Rami Yacoub worked on a song for a teenage singer from Louisiana. The track was called "...Baby One More Time". The song has often been reported to have been offered to TLC first. Britney Spears sang it in Stockholm, and the record came out in the fall of 1998.

The timing was almost cruel. Denniz PoP, who had been fighting stomach cancer, died in August 1998 at 35, only weeks before the song reached the public. Cheiron wound down by 2000, and Martin carried the sound out of the studio and into the wider world.

Spears's single opened a long run for him. He wrote or co-wrote hits for the Backstreet Boys, NSYNC, Kelly Clarkson, Katy Perry, Pink, Taylor Swift, the Weeknd and many others. The same pattern repeated again and again: a clean beat, a chorus that arrives early and an economy that leaves no room for filler.

Many of those hits borrowed from rock, dance and country, but the method stayed the same. A Swedish studio with a few keyboards and a lot of tape had taught the world's radio stations how a pop song should be built.

stories.title: Adele's 21
stories.dek: A breakup, a piano and the album that won six Grammys
stories.body:
In 2008 Adele was a 19-year-old from London with a debut album, 19, and a gift for sounding older than her years. A few years later she was in the studio with a heartbreak that would make an even bigger record.

She has said that the song "Rolling in the Deep" began on the day after a breakup, when she walked into a London studio angry. Producer Paul Epworth, who had worked with indie bands before, built a pounding beat while she sang in a low, furious voice. They have said the core of the song came together quickly, and the finished record kept its stomping drum and gospel shout of a chorus.

Her new album, named 21 for her age, was shaped by the same breakup. It was recorded in several places, with different producers, including Rick Rubin, who helped on some tracks. Rubin has been known for stripped-down work, and several songs on the album have little more than piano, guitar and her voice. The ballad "Someone Like You" was written with Dan Wilson, who earlier led the band Semisonic, after she learned that her former partner had moved on. At the 2011 BRIT Awards she sang it at a piano with no band, and the song surged up the charts in the days afterward.

Adele was not a typical star. She relied on her voice and a plain-spoken manner, and the album stayed on charts around the world for years. Then her voice failed her. In late 2011, after a hemorrhage on a vocal cord, she cancelled tour dates and had surgery. When she returned at the 2012 Grammy Awards, she sang "Rolling in the Deep" and won six awards for the album and its songs, including Album of the Year.

The result was a record about a private heartache that millions of listeners took for their own, and one more proof that a plain voice and a good song can still beat the biggest production.

stories.title: Believe and Auto-Tune
stories.dek: The robotic voice that came from a seismic engineer
stories.body:
In 1998 Cher was 52 years old and had been famous for more than three decades. She was an unlikely star for the dance clubs of the new decade. But her label gave her a new song, "Believe", and a pair of British producers, Mark Taylor and Brian Rawling, who had an idea.

The song was written by several people, including members of a British songwriting group. When the producers recorded Cher's vocal, they ran it through a piece of software called Auto-Tune. The program had come out in 1997 and was meant to be invisible, quietly nudging a singer's off-key notes into place. Taylor and Rawling instead pushed the setting to its extreme, so that her voice jumped from note to note in a robotic step. The effect was strange and exciting, and it sounded like nothing else on radio.

The software's creator was an engineer named Andy Hildebrand, who had come to music from the oil business, where he analyzed seismic data. The same math could find the pitch of a voice, and he built it into a plug-in.

The producers were worried that other studios would copy the sound, so they said, for a time, that they had used a vocoder or a similar device. Cher also faced doubts from her label, which reportedly asked for a different treatment. She is said to have refused, telling executives that the song should stay as it was. The record came out in the fall of 1998 and became a hit in dozens of countries.

Soon, other singers were using the effect on purpose. In the years that followed, hip-hop and R&B singers such as T-Pain turned it into a style. By the 2010s Auto-Tune was everywhere, both as a hidden fix and a creative choice.

For Cher, "Believe" was a second wind. She had helped turn a tool made to hide errors into a new instrument, and a quirk of software became part of pop's sound.

stories.title: Beychella
stories.dek: Two weekends in the desert, April 2018.
stories.body:
In 2017 Beyonce was scheduled to headline the Coachella festival in California, but she postponed because she was pregnant with twins. The festival organizers waited, and in April 2018 she took the stage as the headliner on two weekends, April 14 and April 21. She was widely noted as the first Black woman to headline the festival. Fans quickly gave the show a nickname, Beychella.

The performance was built around the idea of a homecoming at a historically Black college or university. Beyonce was surrounded by a marching band of drummers, brass players and dancers, along with step teams and a choir, and the stage was arranged in the form of a huge pyramid of risers. She wore custom outfits inspired by Egyptian queens and by collegiate sportswear, with Greek letters on sweatshirts and jerseys. The show drew on traditions of marching bands and fraternity and sorority steps, which are part of Black American college life.

The set stretched to more than two hours, and it moved from a high-energy opening to slower, more reflective moments. Songs from her many albums were reworked with live brass and drums, and the sound had a thick, funky quality. Crazy in Love, her breakout hit with Jay-Z from 2003, took on a new, driving energy with the horns. Jay-Z himself made an appearance, and a reunion of Destiny's Child, with Kelly Rowland and Michelle Williams, thrilled the crowd. Beyonce also included Lift Every Voice and Sing, a song often called the Black national anthem.

Beyonce has said that the show took months of preparation and that she wanted to bring the culture of historically Black colleges to a mainstream stage. She also said that she had to rebuild her strength after the birth of her twins, and she rehearsed with intensity.

A year later, in April 2019, she released a Netflix film called Homecoming and an accompanying live album. The film took viewers behind the scenes, showing rehearsals, costume fittings and the effort needed to bring so many performers together.

Beychella was a statement about the power of tradition and the ambition of a pop star. For the audience in the desert, and for the millions who watched online, it was one of the high points of the decade.

stories.title: Adele at the Royal Albert Hall
stories.dek: One woman, a big room and a hard-won voice in September 2011.
stories.body:
By September 2011 Adele was a global star. Her second album, 21, had made her one of the most popular singers in the world, and Rolling in the Deep and Someone Like You were being played everywhere. In that month she took the stage at the Royal Albert Hall in London for a concert that was filmed for release.

The Royal Albert Hall is a Victorian concert hall that holds thousands of people, and it has hosted generations of famous performers. It is a daunting place for a singer who is standing alone, but Adele seemed relaxed. Between songs she chatted with the audience in her warm London voice, joking about her nerves, her love life and her habit of swearing. The mix of humor and emotional power became part of her image.

The show was staged with great care but little fuss. A small band stood behind her, and she sang from the middle of the stage. The set drew from both of her albums, including Rolling in the Deep, Chasing Pavements and Someone Like You, and it ended with the audience on its feet. Her voice rose over everything without strain, and she let silence fall between songs so that the room could listen.

The recording was released as a DVD and Blu-ray in November 2011 under the title Live at the Royal Albert Hall. It also became a way for fans to see Adele at a time when her schedule was falling apart. In the autumn of 2011 she was forced to cancel tour dates because of problems with her voice, and in November she had surgery to treat a vocal cord hemorrhage. The concert film caught her at a high point just before the break.

Adele rested for months, and she returned to public life in February 2012, when she performed at the Grammy Awards and won six trophies. The surgery had succeeded, and her voice recovered.

The Royal Albert Hall show remains a favorite among fans of her early years. It reminds listeners that the power of Adele's songs, with their plain words and big choruses, comes from the voice and the feeling behind it. No special effects were needed.

covers.title: Nothing Compares 2 U
covers.album: I Do Not Want What I Haven't Got
covers.note: Prince wrote it for the Family, a band he assembled, for their 1985 album. O'Connor's 1990 version reached number one in the US and the UK.

covers.title: I Will Always Love You
covers.note: Parton wrote it as a farewell to her mentor Porter Wagoner. Houston's version for The Bodyguard spent fourteen weeks at number one in the US.

covers.title: Mad World
covers.note: Roland Orzabal wrote it, and Tears for Fears released it in 1982 as an upbeat synth single. The slowed piano version for the film Donnie Darko was the UK Christmas number one in 2003.

covers.title: Valerie
covers.note: The Liverpool band the Zutons released it on Tired of Hanging Around in 2006. Ronson's brassy arrangement with Amy Winehouse followed a year later.

covers.title: Have I Told You Lately
covers.note: Morrison released it on Avalon Sunset in 1989. Stewart recorded it for Vagabond Heart in 1991, and a live version from his Unplugged...and Seated album reached the US top five in 1993.

covers.title: Lovesong
covers.note: Robert Smith wrote it for The Cure's 1989 album Disintegration, reportedly as a wedding gift to his wife. Adele turned it into a slow acoustic number on 21.

covers.title: All by Myself
covers.note: Carmen based the verses on a theme from Rachmaninoff's Second Piano Concerto and released it in 1975. Dion's 1996 version made it a big hit again.

covers.title: Don't Cha
covers.note: Tori Alamaze recorded it in 2004, but her version was little heard. The Dolls' 2005 recording, with Busta Rhymes, was a worldwide hit.
